01.r: Introduces the words of God that follow.
01.n: Gesenius: the phrase 'thus says Jehovah' is very frequent, especially at the beginning of communications from God.

02.n: The form is a perfect, 'has said'; English idiom uses the present. YLT keeps the past, 'said'.

03.n: The brief's lexicon: a title, spoken in place of the divine name out of reverence.

04.r: The personal name of Israel's God.
04.n: The divine name, here pointed with the vowels of the word for 'God' because 'Lord' stands just before it (so the brief's lexicon). Our register writes the name 'the LORD'; after 'the Lord' we write 'GOD', in capitals, as the BSB and JPS do, to avoid 'the Lord the LORD'. The ASV and YLT say 'Jehovah'.

05.r: God calls a halt: the princes have gone far enough.
05.n: The word means 'much, many', and the brief's lexicon lists 'abundant, enough' among its senses. 'Much for you' is a Hebrew way of saying 'you have had enough of this'.

07.r: The rulers of Israel addressed as a body.
07.n: Gesenius: literally 'lifted up', and so a prince, a general name used both of kings and of the leaders of tribes, including the prince in this part of Ezekiel.

09.r: The harm the princes do to their people.

10.r: The ruin that violence leaves behind.
10.n: Gesenius gives first 'violence, oppression of the weak', and by extension wealth obtained by violence; the brief's lexicon gives 'havoc, violence, destruction'. We use 'havoc' to keep it apart from the word before it, which we render 'violence'.

11.r: Get rid of the violence and havoc.
11.n: The causative of 'turn aside': 'make it turn aside', so 'remove'. The command is plural, to all the princes. The two nouns stand before it in the Hebrew, for emphasis.

12.r: Fair judgment, what rulers owe their people.
12.n: The 'and' that opens this clause in our English belongs to this word. Gesenius gives first 'judgment', the act of judging; BDB adds 'justice, right'.

13.n: The brief's lexicon lists 'righteousness in government, of judge, ruler, king' among its senses, which fits princes here.

14.n: A plural command. Like 'remove', it comes after its objects in the Hebrew.

15.r: Take the burden of evictions off the people.
15.n: The causative of 'rise': 'make rise', 'lift up'. BDB records that it also means 'take away, remove'. With 'off' it pictures a weight lifted off the people.

16.r: The princes' practice of driving people out of their holdings.
16.n: The brief's lexicon: expulsion, dispossession, act of expulsion; BDB: expulsion, violence. The word occurs only here. The KJV, JPS and ASV say 'exactions', which suggests a levy; the Hebrew speaks of putting people out, which is what the BSB's 'dispossessing' says.

17.r: The evictions rest on the people like a load.

18.r: God claims the dispossessed as his own people.

19.r: Seals the command as God's own word.
19.n: A noun, 'utterance of'; the brief's lexicon notes that it nearly always stands before the divine name. YLT keeps the noun: 'an affirmation of'.

20.r: God's title, as at the start of the verse.

21.r: The divine name, as at the start of the verse.

01.n: Τάδε is the neuter plural of ὅδε, 'this': 'these things says the Lord'. The brief gives no dictionary form.

04.n: The Greek renders 'the Lord GOD' as Κύριος θεός, 'the Lord God'.

05.n: ἱκανόω, to make sufficient: 'let it suffice you', the wording the KJV follows.

07.n: ἀφηγέομαι, to lead: 'the leaders of Israel'.

11.n: ἀφέλεσθε, 'take away', from ἀφαιρέω; the brief gives no dictionary form.

15.n: ἐξάρατε, 'lift away, remove', from ἐξαίρω; the brief gives no dictionary form.

16.n: καταδυναστεία, oppression, domination by the powerful: the Greek names the abuse more generally than the Hebrew 'evictions'.
